questions.question: Explain the difference between trade discount and cash discount, including how each is recorded, and give the test that separates them.
questions.expected_answer: A trade discount reduces the price before the transaction is recorded — the sale is simply captured at the reduced price and no separate item appears in the books. A cash or settlement discount rewards prompt payment of an existing debt and is recorded: discount allowed as an expense when granted to debtors, discount received as income when granted by creditors. The test: price reduced before recording — trade, invisible; existing debt settled for less — cash, recorded.

questions.question: Contrast financial and managerial accounting across audience, direction and rules, using one example question for each branch.
questions.expected_answer: Financial accounting serves outsiders — banks, SARS, the owner formally — reports on the past, and follows GAAP so statements can be trusted and compared: 'What profit did the shop make last year?' Managerial accounting serves insiders, looks forward, and follows no external rulebook because usefulness is its only test: 'Should the shop open a second branch next year?' Same underlying figures, different audience, direction and rules.

questions.question: Describe what happens in the books when Sipho sells a backpack for R450 that cost R270 under the perpetual system, and why this system turns a stocktake into a check rather than a discovery.
questions.expected_answer: Two things are recorded at the moment of sale: the sale at selling price R450, and cost of sales R270 moving out of Trading Stock — so gross profit of R180 is visible immediately and the stock account always shows what should be on the shelf. Because the records state what ought to be on hand, a physical count tests them: a shortfall like R1 800 becomes a named, investigable gap, whereas the periodic system would silently assume the missing goods were sold.
